title: {{NAME}} and the Iron Crown Championship
moral: The greatest victory is not the one you win for yourself, but the one you make possible for everyone around you.

pages.content:
The kingdom of Ironholm was an unusual place to hold a football championship. Its streets were paved with hammered bronze, its market stalls sold gears alongside bread, and its ruling princess, Kira, had personally designed the stadium in which the championship would be played, including a retractable roof that opened like an enormous metal flower.

{{NAME}} had arrived in Ironholm the way visitors usually did, which was by following an invitation that appeared on his doorstep in an envelope made of beaten copper, sealed with wax in the shape of a gear-within-a-crown. The invitation requested his presence as the final player for the visiting team in the Iron Crown Championship. It said nothing else, which {{NAME}} found both impressive and slightly nerve-wracking.

The stadium, from the outside, looked like a cathedral built by someone who loved both architecture and engineering in equal measure. The walls were carved with scenes from famous matches, each one executed in loving metalwork, and above the main gate stood a statue of a robot in a goalkeeper's stance, one arm extended, one leg raised, frozen at the moment of the save.

Princess Kira stood at the gate itself, arms crossed, wearing a crown that appeared to be welded rather than jewelled, and a training kit in Ironholm's colours of deep bronze and white.

'You're the last piece,' she said. 'Come on, then. Training starts in six minutes.'

pages.content:
The robot goalkeeper was named Brex, and he was not a statue. He moved, slowly and with great deliberation, the way very large things move when they are trying not to break smaller things by accident.

Brex had been built by Princess Kira's mother, the previous queen, as a birthday gift to the city, and he had been playing goalkeeper for Ironholm's team ever since. His saves were not especially athletic. They were mathematical. He calculated every trajectory, accounted for every spin and wind factor, and positioned himself with such precise certainty that shots had a way of simply arriving in his hands rather than having to be caught.

'He rarely dives,' Princess Kira explained, as they watched Brex stop eight consecutive shots without moving more than three steps in any direction. 'He doesn't need to. He thinks too fast.'

{{NAME}} studied Brex. The robot's amber sensor-eyes tracked the ball with absolute focus. But once, between shots, those eyes swivelled briefly to where a group of children were watching from the stands, and something in Brex's posture changed, just fractionally, from mechanical precision to something warmer.

'He likes having an audience,' {{NAME}} said.

Princess Kira looked at him with new interest. 'Most people say he doesn't feel anything,' she said.

'Most people,' {{NAME}} replied, 'are not paying attention.'

pages.content:
The championship match arrived like a thunderstorm, loud and sudden and entirely present.

Ironholm's opponents, the team from the neighbouring kingdom of Vethara, were good. Very good. They pressed from the first whistle, a coordinated, relentless unit that moved with the efficiency of a machine themselves, though a human one.

{{NAME}} played central midfield, the engine room, and he threw himself into it. He tracked every run, intercepted three passes in the first quarter, and had the ball moving quickly enough that Vethara's defensive shape never quite settled. Princess Kira, playing up front, was direct and precise, converting two chances that lesser forwards would have overthought.

But then Brex was tested.

In the seventy-second minute, Vethara broke fast, three against one, and their striker struck the ball with tremendous power toward the top corner. Not the kind of chance Brex could stand still for. Not mathematical. Purely athletic.

Brex dived.

The entire stadium inhaled.

Brex's enormous bronze hand closed around the ball with a sound like a gear clicking into place, and he landed on his side, skidding across the goal mouth, the ball held safe against his chest.

The children in the stands made a sound that was not a cheer so much as a sudden collective expression of pure delight.

Brex held the ball up and let them see it.

Just for a moment.

pages.content:
Two-two. Extra time. And Brex had gone still.

Not the calculating stillness of before. Something different. {{NAME}} jogged to the goal and found the princess already there, one hand on the robot's forearm.

'His power reserves,' she said quietly. 'He gave everything on that dive. He won't be able to play extra time at full capacity.'

Brex's amber eyes flickered. They focused on {{NAME}} with an expression that, in a human face, would have been apologetic.

'Tell me what you need,' {{NAME}} said.

Brex's voice, usually as smooth as clockwork, came out in slow measured bursts. 'Two saves. If they score twice I cannot hold. I need the team to protect the channels.'

Princess Kira straightened. She looked at {{NAME}}, and he looked back at her, and something wordless was agreed between them.

They spent extra time defending with everything. {{NAME}} threw himself in front of shots that Brex should have saved, taking the impact himself, scrambling the ball clear. Princess Kira dropped back from her striker's position and patrolled the penalty area with an intensity that left no gaps.

Brex made his two saves. Exactly two. Both moments of pure, flickering calculation with amber eyes that were dimming but not done.

Then Princess Kira went forward for the last time, received the ball from {{NAME}}'s tired boot, and put it away.

The metal flower roof opened. The whole stadium saw the stars.

pages.content:
The Iron Crown was a beautiful thing, even up close. It was neither iron nor gold but something in between, warm to the touch, and it was passed around the team before Princess Kira placed it in the display case that would hold it for another year.

Then she lifted a smaller crown from beneath the case, a simple bronze circlet worked with tiny gear-and-ball motifs, and gave it to Brex. He held it in both huge hands and turned it over very slowly, as though something needed to be understood about it before it could be worn.

Brex placed it on his own domed head.

The children in the stands, who had never left, erupted again.

{{NAME}} sat on the pitch with his legs stretched out, too tired for anything more energetic than breathing, watching Brex turn very slowly in the stadium lights so every part of the crowd could see the circlet properly.

Princess Kira sat down beside him with an undignified thump.

'He's been playing for this city for sixteen years,' she said. 'Nobody ever gave him a crown before.'

{{NAME}} watched Brex's amber eyes, blazing bright again now that the match pressure was gone. 'He noticed every one of them, though,' {{NAME}} said. 'Every single match.'

He walked home slowly under warm stars, the scuff of his scarlet cleats ringing softly on Ironholm's bronze streets, already wondering whether the copper envelope would appear on his doorstep again next year.
